Author: @furiousfemmeyazeth3362
Content:
A valiant attempt and a most delicious interpretation. Although risnatu is not breadcrumbs, but a fermented & brined prepared ingredient; crushed millet and/or barley berries, yeast, mashed dates and/or figs, with wine vinegar and salt. Some regional variations exempted the dates and figs in lieu of honey and beans -- even juniper berries; in many parts of Anatolia, fermented fish (similar to garum) was used instead. Often times risnatu was created from otherwise discarded ingredients, and thus was a way to reduce wastage. 

Best to think of the ingredient as being similar to Chinese fermented broadbean. The flavor profile should be umami, sweet, somewhat smoky, slightly piquant, and usually incorporates notes of wood.

Author: @nimarus3118
Content:
So I asked Grok about Risnatu and this is what it had to say:
Yes, researchers have identified risnatu as a type of pasta-like food used in ancient Babylonian cuisine, based on translations of cuneiform tablets from the Yale Babylonian Collection, dating back to around 1750 BCE. Risnatu, along with its synonym bapirru, was made from a dough of flour (typically wheat or barley, native to Mesopotamia), water, and sometimes fat. The dough was kneaded, grated against a sieve to create small flakes or crumbs, and then poached in a broth or stew, resembling what we might call "pasta grattugiata" (grated pasta) in Italian or modern Iraqi soup noodles like rishta.
Risnatu served multiple purposes in Babylonian dishes: it added texture, acted as a thickener for stews, and could be used like a cracker or dumpling to accompany or absorb sauces. For example, in recipes like the Babylonian lamb stew (Immeru Šuḫutinnu), risnatu is listed as an ingredient, often added to enhance the dish’s consistency or as a crunchy garnish, similar to croutons. The exact preparation varied—risnatu could be boiled like dumplings, baked like hardtack, or pan-fried like crackers, depending on the dish.
Modern recreations, such as those by culinary historians and scholars like Gojko Barjamovic and Nawal Nasrallah, suggest risnatu was a versatile, staple component in Mesopotamian cooking, reflecting a sophisticated culinary tradition that connects to modern Middle Eastern stews and pasta dishes.

Author: @vorvayne5935
Content: My partner comes from Syria and food like this is still eaten today (ancient Babylon was on the outer age of Syria/into Iraq iirc); we *strongly* suspect that this dish was in fact made with yoghurt, because 1) milk is very little used in cooking in that region, especially in older dishes, because before refrigeration it went off in about ten minutes, and 2) in many regions - including the Syria/Iraq border - the word for milk and yoghurt is the same, everyone calls it lebne, everything is lebne unless you want to really definitely specify milk. Oh and also 3) many dishes with this same formula - a stew with meat, onions, garlic and yoghurt - are still common in Syria. It's often "poor people food" because lebne is cheap and plentiful and you don't need to use much meat if you can't afford much and the dish will still be good and substantial with yoghurt.

Content:
Fun fact about that fat tail sheep: in Judaism, the laws of kashrut forbid consumption of many types of fat, called "chelev," notably suet. Chelev is also a term just generally describing "the good stuff," like in the phrase "the fat of the land." The fat in fat tail sheep is referred to in some places as being "chelev," leading to some discourse among ancient rabbis over whether or not it is forbidden, but they concluded that "No, it's 'chelev' as in it's delicious. Go ahead."

Of course this whole recipe is forbidden anyway because it has dairy and meat together 😅

Author: @msxy9594
Content: Sounds to me more like a recipe for Mansaf.(Lamb in Joghurt Sauce) The ancient Canaanites and the Beduins traditonally made this dish on festive days and this dish is known allover Middle East! Its still very popular in Jordan these days. The Lamb was originally  cooked in fermented Milk but today one can use plain Joghurt that is mixed with water (tthat will taste about the same) and the spice used is SAFFRON... Perhaps "Risnatu" was a old Babylonian word for Saffron?... Its usually served with Rice (or in older times with Bulgur) and garnished with nuts. Then this dish would make more sense. Im 99 % positive this is an ancient recipe for Mansaf!
